title: Duties 1–2: assessment, treatment & referral
blurb: Your part in assessment, diagnosis, treatment and referral: what you do, what the dentist does, and how to talk about it within scope.
question: The assessor asks: "Talk me through your role when a new patient comes in for an examination and ends up needing a referral to a specialist." How do you describe what you did without claiming the dentist's job?

teach.body: Duty 1 is to "undertake routine dental nursing clinical and technical procedures and tasks relevant to the assessment, and diagnosis of patients". Duty 2 is the same for "treatment planning and onward referral". The key words are "relevant to". The GDC Scope of Practice says dental nurses do not diagnose disease or plan treatment, and work under the prescription, direction or delegation of a dentist or other registrant. Your job is to make assessment and treatment safe, accurate and smooth.

teach.caption: Taking radiographs is an additional skill that needs a separate qualification. Without it, your part is processing and managing the images.

Dictated: "36 caries, 46 missing, 21 crown, 16 filled, 38 for extraction." Accurate charting depends on knowing your FDI notation and tooth anatomy. One wrong digit could mean treatment on the wrong tooth.

teach.h: Why the medical history matters so much
teach.body: A comprehensive, contemporaneous history is the foundation of safe care. Medicines, allergies and conditions change what the dentist can safely do and how the team prepares for emergencies. Your part is to record it accurately, check it is up to date in line with practice policy, and make sure the dentist knows about anything new before treatment starts. Never assume a patient's history is unchanged since their last visit.

teach.h: History items and why they matter
head: Item
Why it matters
rows: Latex, antibiotics or materials can cause a reaction
Can affect jaw healing after extractions
Be ready for the matching emergency

teach.body: You need anatomy to chart accurately, to retract the tongue and cheeks safely, to place the aspirator where it protects the airway without triggering a gag, and to understand what the dentist means by terms such as "mesial", "caries into dentine" or "mental foramen". Recognising normal anatomy, and how it varies between patients, also helps you notice when something looks or sounds different and needs the dentist's attention.

steps.label: Dentist diagnoses and plans
steps.sub: Explains options; patient gives valid consent

steps.label: Chairside support
steps.sub: Aspirate, mix materials, monitor and reassure

teach.caption: Medical emergencies and acute oral conditions sit here too: you help identify and manage them with the team.

teach.body: Both duties rely on clear spoken, written and electronic communication with the team. That means telling the dentist straight away about a change in history, passing on what a patient said while you were alone with them (a long-standing ulcer, a worry about a bruise, a sudden swelling), giving a clear handover, and making sure referral letters reach the right service. If a patient shows signs of abuse or neglect, you follow the practice safeguarding procedure.

teach.text: In the discussion, never say "I diagnosed", "I decided the treatment" or "I told the patient it was nothing". Say what the dentist decided, then what YOU did: "The dentist diagnosed caries in 36; I recorded it and prepared the surgery."

items: Duties 1 and 2 are tasks relevant to assessment, diagnosis, treatment planning and referral.
Dental nurses don't diagnose or plan treatment; they work under prescription, direction or delegation.
Accurate history and charting keep patients safe; flag every change to the dentist.
Anatomy underpins charting, safe retraction and aspiration, and noticing abnormalities.
Communicate clearly with colleagues: handovers, concerns, referrals, safeguarding.

summary: You can now explain duties 1 and 2 in your own words, separate the dentist's role from yours at each stage from history-taking to referral, explain why accurate history and charting matter, and describe your clinical examples using language that stays within the dental nurse's scope.

A.q: During an examination the dentist says, "Lower left first molar, occlusal caries." What is your role?
options: Confirm the diagnosis by checking the tooth yourself
Ask the patient which treatment option they would prefer
Wait and add it to the notes at the end of the day
Record it accurately on the chart against tooth 36
A.why: Recording charting as dictated, accurately and at the time, is a core duty 1 task. The lower left first molar is 36 in FDI notation.

whyNot.0: Confirming a diagnosis is the dentist's role, not the nurse's.
whyNot.1: Discussing treatment options follows the dentist's diagnosis and plan.
whyNot.2: Records must be contemporaneous, made at the time, not later.

A.q: While updating a patient's medical history before an extraction, you learn she has just started an anticoagulant. What should you do?
options: Tell the dentist before treatment begins
Cancel the appointment and rebook her
Note it and mention it at the next visit
Advise her to stop the tablets for a day
A.why: Anticoagulants increase bleeding risk, so the dentist must know before starting. Flagging changes is part of supporting safe assessment and treatment.

whyNot.1: Deciding whether treatment goes ahead is the dentist's clinical decision.
whyNot.2: This affects today's extraction, so waiting is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Giving advice about prescribed medicines is outside a dental nurse's scope and could be dangerous.

A.q: Which task is part of a dental nurse's normal scope after registration, without an additional qualification?
options: Justifying which radiograph the patient needs
Taking the radiograph and pressing the exposure
Processing and managing digital radiographs
Explaining what the radiograph shows
A.why: The GDC Scope of Practice lists monitoring and processing digital images and dental radiographs as a routine dental nurse task.

whyNot.0: Justification is the IR(ME)R practitioner's role, usually the dentist.
whyNot.1: Taking radiographs needs specific training and certification as an additional skill.
whyNot.3: Interpreting a radiograph is part of diagnosis, which dental nurses don't do.

B.q: While you set up, a patient mentions a sore patch under his tongue that hasn't healed for a month. What is the best response?
options: Reassure him that most mouth ulcers are harmless
Make sure the dentist knows before the examination
Suggest he buys an ulcer gel from the pharmacy
Tell him to see his GP if it is still there next month
B.why: A non-healing ulcer can be a sign of oral cancer. Passing it on so the dentist can assess it, and refer early if needed, is part of duties 1 and 2.

whyNot.0: Reassuring him is effectively a diagnosis, and it could delay an urgent referral.
whyNot.2: Recommending treatment without assessment is outside scope and delays diagnosis.
whyNot.3: Delaying another month is unsafe; the dentist should assess it today.

B.q: The assessor asks why a full, up-to-date medical history matters. Which answer is best?
options: It is mainly needed so the practice can claim NHS fees
It lets the dental nurse decide whether treatment is safe today
It only really matters for patients over the age of 65
Medicines and conditions affect safe treatment and emergencies
B.why: Medicines, allergies and conditions change what is safe and which emergencies the team must be ready for, which is why the history must be complete and current.

whyNot.0: Fee claims are not the reason; patient safety is.
whyNot.1: The dentist decides on safety; the nurse records and flags.
whyNot.2: Every patient's history matters, whatever their age.

B.q: The dentist asks you to chart the upper right first molar as having a filling. Which FDI number do you record?
B.why: In FDI notation the upper right quadrant is 1, and the first molar is tooth 6, so it is 16.

whyNot.0: 26 is the upper left first molar.
whyNot.1: 36 is the lower left first molar.
whyNot.3: 46 is the lower right first molar.

C.q: Which statement describes duty 2 in a way that stays within a dental nurse's scope?
options: "The dentist planned the extraction; I prepared and supported"
"I planned the extraction and then the dentist carried it out"
"I chose the specialist and wrote the referral myself"
"I decided the patient needed a root filling, not a crown"
C.why: The dentist plans treatment; the nurse prepares, supports, monitors and arranges follow-up as prescribed.

whyNot.1: Planning treatment is outside the dental nurse's scope.
whyNot.2: The dentist decides on the referral; the nurse can prepare the paperwork.
whyNot.3: Choosing between treatments is treatment planning, which nurses don't do.

C.q: A patient collapses in the chair. Which response best fits the dental nurse's role in duty 2?
options: Wait outside until the dentist asks for help
Fetch the emergency kit and oxygen and support the team
Phone the patient's family before anything else
Give an emergency drug of your own choosing straight away
C.why: Dental nurses work with the team to identify, assess and manage medical emergencies, which includes bringing the kit and oxygen and following the team's lead.

whyNot.0: Waiting wastes vital time; you are part of the emergency team.
whyNot.2: Calling family is not a priority while the patient needs urgent care.
whyNot.3: Emergency drugs are given in line with protocol as a team, not chosen alone.

C.q: Which of these is NOT a duty 1 or duty 2 task for a dental nurse?
options: Recording the patient's oral health assessment
Mixing a material to the operator's instructions
Arranging follow-up care as the dentist prescribed
Telling a patient what their radiograph shows
C.why: Explaining what a radiograph shows is interpreting it, which is part of diagnosis and outside a dental nurse's scope.

whyNot.0: Recording an oral health assessment is a duty 1 task.
whyNot.1: Preparing and mixing materials is a duty 2 task.
whyNot.2: Arranging follow-up as prescribed is a duty 2 task.

reteach.title: The pilot and the co-pilot
reteach.question: If the dentist is the pilot, what makes a good co-pilot?

blocks.body: A pilot decides the route and flies the plane. The co-pilot runs the checklists, reads out the instruments, spots warning lights and handles the radio. A flight is only safe with both. The dentist diagnoses and plans. You run the checks (medical history, records, decontaminated kit), call out what you notice (a new medicine, a worrying ulcer), and keep communication flowing (charting, referrals, handovers). You never take the controls, but the flight depends on you.

blocks.text: A co-pilot who sees a warning light and says nothing has failed. Flagging changes and concerns to the dentist is one of the most important things you do in duties 1 and 2.

explain.body: Recording history, charting and oral health assessments, preparing records and images, processing radiographs, reassuring anxious patients and noticing safeguarding concerns. The dentist examines and diagnoses.

test.q: Which is a duty 1 task for a dental nurse?
options: Deciding that a broken tooth is non-restorable
Recording the charting dictated by the dentist
Choosing which radiograph should be taken
Diagnosing gum disease from the BPE scores
test.why: Accurately recording the dentist's charting supports assessment and diagnosis, which is duty 1.

whyNot.2: Choosing (justifying) a radiograph is the IR(ME)R practitioner's role.
whyNot.3: Interpreting BPE scores to diagnose is the clinician's role.

explain.body: It must be complete and contemporaneous. Medicines, allergies and conditions affect safe treatment and emergency readiness. Record it, keep it current, and tell the dentist about changes before treatment.

test.q: A patient's history shows a new latex allergy. What is the most important reason to flag it before treatment?
options: To update the practice database
To prevent an allergic reaction
To change the appointment fee
To meet the CQC inspection rules
test.why: Flagging the allergy lets the team avoid latex and prevent a reaction, which could be life-threatening.

whyNot.0: Updating the database matters, but patient safety is the main reason.
whyNot.3: Inspections check safety systems, but the reason here is the patient's safety.

explain.body: After the dentist plans treatment and the patient consents, you prepare the surgery, provide chairside support, monitor the patient, help manage emergencies, arrange follow-up as prescribed and prepare referral paperwork.

test.q: The dentist decides a patient needs a specialist referral. What is the nurse's appropriate part?
options: Choosing which specialist service to refer to
Explaining the diagnosis to the patient
Deciding how urgent the referral should be
Preparing the paperwork and sending it securely
test.why: The dentist decides on the referral and its urgency; the nurse can prepare the paperwork for the dentist to sign and make sure it is sent securely and recorded.

whyNot.0: Choosing the specialist is part of the dentist's clinical decision.
whyNot.1: Explaining a diagnosis is the dentist's role.
whyNot.2: Urgency is a clinical judgement made by the dentist.

explain.body: If a patient tells you something clinically important, such as a non-healing ulcer, a new medicine or a sign of possible abuse, you pass it on promptly and record it. Silence is the risk.

steps.label: Notice
steps.sub: What the patient says or shows

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: In the notes, at the time

test.q: In the waiting room a patient mentions she has started new tablets for her heart. What should you do?
options: Make sure the dentist knows and the history is updated
Ask her to bring the tablet box to her next visit
Look the drug up yourself and decide if it matters
Nothing, as heart tablets don't affect dentistry
test.why: A new medicine must be added to the history and passed to the dentist before treatment, because it may affect safety.

whyNot.1: The information is needed today, not next time.
whyNot.2: Judging clinical significance is the dentist's role.
whyNot.3: Many heart medicines, such as anticoagulants, affect dental treatment.
